docs.text: Geography ¶ 1. Is there enough water ¶ 1.1 how much water? ¶ 97% Oceans and seas 3% Freshwater 30% Groundwater 70% Glaciers and ice caps 0.3% surface water (rivers and lakes) 1.2 Where does it come from ¶ Water cycle Water is found mainly in Oceans, Seas, the Atmosphere and the land Water cycles through them through different processes: Water cycle 1.3 freshwater resources globally ¶ Unevenly distributed Some countries face unstable water supply High rainfall -> enough Lower rainfall -> Water scarcity 1.4 Threads to global freshwater resources ¶ inadequate freshwater supply Water scarcity affects over 40% of the world population Why? Higher demand Population increase -> higher demand for freshwater resources globally for domestic and economic activities Higher living standards Water footprint = the level of development More money -> more meat and diary products -> more water comsumption -> larger water footprints Decreasing supply Water pollution Toxic or dirty substance e.g. industrial waste or sewage enters lakes, rivers and groundwater4 -> Cannot be used Climate change Some region recieve less precipitation -> lower freshwater supply 2 How is it in China ¶ Water problems in China Water Scarcity China has a lot of freshwater But not much per capita -> water may not meet people's needs bc imbalance between water supply and demand Regional and sesonal differences North: less water South: more water Winter: less water Flooding and drought Related to the distribution of precipitation Location of freshwater resources Most freshwater resources are obtained from rivers and lakes River basin = Area that precipitation flows into river aka drained by a river Most important: Chang Jiang, Zhu Jiang, Heilong Jiang (From most to least) Wet and Dry regions 32% of land is humid Mainly found in the southern region 53% of land is Semi-arid or arid Mainly found in the nothern and north-western regions South wet, North-western dry Factors of Percipitation Large part of China has monsoon climates Monsoons = winds that change direction seasonally blowing opposite way in summer and winter Summer Land absorb heat quickily -> air becomes hot and rise -> **air pressure low ** Water absorb heat slower than land -> air cooler and sink -> air pressure higher Air moves from high-pressure area to low pressure-area -> blow from sea towards land (southern and eastern part of Asia) Which are onshore winds and summer monsoons carry much moisture -> wet summer Winter Opposite: release heat faster for land / slower for sea Distance from the sea Onshore wind carry moisture Reach inland areas -> moisture lost Eastern coast recieve more percipitation than the inland regions Relation of percipitation to freshwater resources and water problems Precipitation recieved in a place varies with seasons Area affected by monsoon recieve higher rainfall in summer then in winter Distribution is highly uneven Wet season: higher volume of river flow More water in wet season(summer) water scarcity is more severe in winter Dry season longer then normal -> drought rainfall in the wet season is exceptionally high -> flooding 3 Worsening of water scarcity ¶ bc Increasing demand, Decreasing supply 3.1 Why is demand increasing? ¶ Increase in population Continuous population growth -> larger demand for water Economic development Since open policy rapid economic growth Economic activities demand for huge amount of water (e.g. manufacturing, agricultural activities) Water is also use ineffectively Only 1/3 of irrigation water is used effectively freshwater resource used to produce one unit of product is way more then more developed countries Rise in living standards Rapid economic development -> income increase -> living standard improve Demand for more food and consumer goods -> more water is needed for different uses Low cost of water Cost of water is low Not enough economic incentive for water users to save water Many people are not aware of the importance of water conservation -> waste water 3.2 Water supply decrease ¶ Water pollution Rapid population growth + economic development -> higher use of water resoruces -> increase in the discharge in sewage (doubled from 1980 to 2015) If sewage is discharged into lakes and rivers w/o treatment -> water pollution Some farmers apply too much chemical (pesticides, fertilizers) Excess chemicals + untreated animal waste may be washed into rivers and lakes by rainfall -> cause water pollution + pollute groundwater Depletion of Groundwater Water stored underground From water that seep into the ground Major source of freshwater supply if lakes and river are not enough -> dig wells Nothern China freshwater resources are not enough to meet the demand for water People rely on groundwater natural groundwater recharge is small Overdrawing groundwater will reduce groundwater storage -> further decrease freshwater supply Avalibility is a security issue -> must have a secure water supply 4 Problem of drought ¶ 4.1 What is it ¶ Rainfall in an area is much lower then normal for a long period of time A natural hazard (if a area is always dry its arid ) 4.2 Impacts of drought in China ¶ On people Farming Lack of water for irrigation / pastures -> Crop faliure, livestock die, farm production drops -> food shortages Industry : Lack of water for processing + cooling: Industrial production will decline Power generation : Water level drop -> hydroelectric power (HEP) production drop Transport: Water transport will be disrupted Daily domestic use Not enough water to use May need to carry out water rationing(restrict water supply) Will cause inconvenience and affect people's health On environment Lakes and rivers dry up -> Cut-off of river X vegatiation -> topsoil blown away -> **soil erosion ** -> intensify desertification (makes land unproductive) -> Sandstorm will be more common plants and animals die -> ecosystem adversely affected 4.3 Where does drought usually occur ¶ X western part Mainly found in the nothern and southern part of China 4.4 Causes of drought ¶ Physical factors (environmental) Variation in rainfall Drought is related to rainfall variability Large part of china is affected by monsoon Timing and strength vary between years Wet summer monsoon come late / dry winter monsoon come early Weak summer monsoon: carry less moisture High temperature Higher temperature -> higher evaporation rates Human factors Human induced climate change human activilies emit Green House Gases into the atmosphere -> climate change -> rainfall in China decreasing High water consumption Water cannot meet the demand even in normal years -> Overdrawing of groundwater Water recieved is below normal -> water avalible is even less -> Drought intensified Reduced water supply Water wastage and water pollution -> decrease in freshwater supply -> intensifies drought 5 Ways of tackling water scarcity ¶ 5.1 China's effort ¶ Increasing supply Building dams and resivoris Wet season: reservoirs behind the dams can store rainwater and river water Dry season: Water released to provide a reliable and adequate source of freshwater use Controlling water pollution Clean up polluted water and lakes: Pass laws and provide money Treat sewage before discharge: Improve sewage management + build new sewage treatment works Reduce discharge Close polluting factories Educate the public Raise water charges Control use of chemicals reuse wastewater purify sewage to recycled water -> More water is drinkable in China Reducing demand Save water on farms Adopt drip irrigation Use plastic films to reduce evaporation of soil water Prevent water leakage Grow drought-resistant crops (peanuts, sweet potatos, millet, sorghum) Reducing industrial and domestic water useage Adopt water-saving technology in industrial production Pass law to shut down factories that don't comply with water-saving regulations Educate people Increase water charges 5.2 Large scale water transfer project ¶ South-North water transfer project Advantages Provide reliable and clean water resources -> support industrial development Maintain wetland + river ecosystem Disadvantages People have to be relocated Less water for Hydroelectric power generation Less water flowing downstream -> Natural habitat of fish downstream is destroyed High construction cost (260M RMB) 6 Problem of flooding ¶ 6.1 What is flooding Rainfall heavy -> river full -> river water flow over bank -> spread onto surrounding land -> flooding 6.2 Impacts of flooding Injury and loss of life Crop faliure Damaging buildings and infastructure (e.g. roads, buildings) Disrupting transport services Disrupting utility services (gas, electricity supplies) Polluting drinking water Spreading diseases 6.3 Area prone to flooding Eastern and southern parts Coastal areas Where major river basins are found 6.4 Causes of flooding ¶ More water in a river than it can hold -> flooding Factors Amount of river flow Holding capacity of river (shallow -> less capacity) Physical factors Heavy rainfall and typhoons Summer monsoons or typhoons bring heavy rain -> + river flow Climate change -> more extreme weather events (typhoons, rainstorms) Low relief + Silting West: Highland East: Coast Rivers in the east flow on gentle slopes -> river flow slows down -> silting (sand and soil is deposited on the river bed) -> reduced holding capacity Human factors Deforestation Cut tree -> soil easily washed away -> silting + more overland flow Farming practises Overgrazing: Gaze a large amount of livestock -> grass does not have time to recover Over-cultivation: Grow crops intensively on slopes -> Soil becomes poor Cause soil erosion -> + silting Reclaiming lakes (pond) Lakes can store water -> regulate flow Reclaiming (for fish ponds, farming, settlement) -> reduced size of lakes Urban development Cover land with concrete -> rain cannot infiltrate -> overland flow Sewer and drain helps divert rainwater quickly -> Reach river in a shorter amount of time -> flooding 7 Ways for controlling flooding ¶ 7.1 Ways of easing problem ¶ Regulating river flow Build dams and reservoirs -> hold and store excess river water -> regulate river flow downstream Restoring storagae function of lakes Prohibit reclamation of land Gived up farmlands and fish ponds that is reclaimed Afforestation Increase infiltration Reduce overland flow -> less rapid water into rivers Increasing holding capacity Preventing silting Reduce soil eurosion Plant trees + control deforestation Terracing ( 梯田 ) -> prevent soil eurosion Stopping grazing Building dykes ( 堤防 ) Raised height of river banks -> prevent water from overflowing Deepening and widening river channels Allows a larger amount of water within the channels Dredging river channels Remove sediemnts -> lower river bed 7.2 Large-scale flood control project ¶ e.g. Three Gorges Dam (Sanxia) Project -> Control flooding in Chang Jiang basin Benifits Store water from upstream areas -> lower risk of flooding Provide cheap HEP (hydroelectricity power) -> relieve air pollution Promote tourism Disavantages Flood large areas of farmland and historicate sites People had to relocate Less fertile soil and less fish -> livelihood of farmers and fishermen is affected Dam collapses -> Serious flooding High construction + maintanance cost Expensive to relocate affected people Harm to ==Industrialization== : Experienced rapid growth and replaced traditional agriculture - ==Urbanization== : People moved from countryside to industrial towns Causes - ==Rise in population== : Increase demand for goods, provided labour - == World trade ==: to meet global demand - Accumulation of ==capital== : Invested on new machines + technological innovations - == Development of science ==: Applied technologies to improve industrial technologies Why start in Britain? - Rich in ==natural resources== (e.g. coal, iron) - Had many ==overseas colonies== - == Enclosure movement ==: Farmers lost their land -> move to cities and worked in factories - Government support - == patent law == to protect rights of inventors - sponsored the == Royal Society == to carry out scientific experiments Major developments - ==Textile industry== was first - Invention of ==steam engine== -> Spread to heavy industries (iron, steel making) - Made Britain rich - Spread to other European countries - Textile industry - Machine was operated by workers in factories - ==' domestic system '== -> ==' factory system '== - Spread to other sectors - Sources of energy - == Steam power == - Watt improved the steam engine - == Coal gas == - powering machines, gas lighting and cooking - == Electricity == - 1870s Edison invented light bulb and first electric power system - ==Oil== - discovered in 19th century - used to power machine - Became the primary energy source - Other industries - Coal mining - Used steam power -> improved efficiency - Iron making - Before industrial revolution: Preferred cast iron bc cheap - Reduced cost of wrought iron and steel -> common industrial materials - Improvement in transportation - Before: Poor roads, used ox-cars, horse carts and sailing ships - Land transportation - == Macadam road == - docs.text: [[Renaissance]] [[Scientific revolution]] - A intellectual and cultural movement between the mid-17th and 18th centuries - Stated that people enjoyed ==natural rights== (equality, liberty) - opposed political and social inequalities Causes - Change of value: Promoted idea of humanism -> applied to social and political aspects - ==Discontent with absolutism== - Absolute rulers promoted the '== divine rights of kings ==' - -> Europeans began to criticize absolutism Ideas - == Laws of nature == - Enjoyed inborn rights of equality and liberty - States and government were set up to protect - == Social contract == - About people and government - ==Locke== + ==Rousseau== suggested - power of government came from people - if government breaks contract and cannot protect people natural rights - people have the right to overthrow - ==Separation of powers== - Montesquieu suggested - ==legislature== , ==executive== and ==judiciary== - prevent absolute rule - ==Constitution + Reforms== - Voltaire suggested - Limit the power of kings and protect people's rights (freedom of speech, press, religion) Spread - academic journals became popular and was a important mean for Europeans to absorb Enlightenment ideas - Publishers were eager to translate and print -> idea became ==widespread== Impact - ==Liberating== minds of European: Awakened Europeans to political system and pursuit to liberty - == Spread == in Europe and Americans -> American Revolution + French Revolution - Enlightenment ideas -> Absolute rulers gave more rights ( Enlightened despots )

economy 2.3 Positive impacts ¶ Multinational corporation MNCs in developed countries carry out regional division of labour ( Outsource low-skilled production processes to developing countries) On Other may offer more favourable business environments, tax incentives, infrastructure Financial institutions hire from all over the world -> outflow of financial processionals from Hong Kong -> Pose Development of mechanical automation and artificial intelligence replaces manual work Service industry accounts for a larger proportion (more employment opportunities and more attractive salaries and benefits) -> Lower supply and demand for workers Financial , professional and other producer services International financial centre with sound legal system Bridge connecting mainland and the world -> longer re-export through Hong Kong -> Weakening Hong Kong's position as a re-export hub in the region Trade conflicts in 2018 -> impact on trade activities and exports and re-exports of goods -> Lower -> less demand for Hong Kong's tourism services Strict entry restrictions and quarantine in 2018 -> number of tourists decrease 3.2 Opportunities ¶ Economic ups and downs ¶ Highly externally oriented and open economy -> easily affected by external factors -> Poses challenges to youth employment Economy recession -> companies hire fewer workers -> youth may have difficulties getting jobs due to low education level or lack of work experience Trends of industrial development ¶ developed into a knowledge economy Develop high-tech and high-value-added industries (e.g. financial technology, information technology) Innovation and technology ( I&T ) Promotes re-industrialisation to develop advanced manufacturing based on new tech Enhances HK's High quality development, create high-quality opportunities for young people Cultural and creative industries 14th 5 year plan supports HK to develop into an East-meets-West centre for international cultural exchange Encourages the development of the arts, culture and creative industries The Policy Address 2022 proposes that government will establish Culture commission -> assist in mapping out a blueprint in Arts and Culture and Creative Industries development Encourages private development projects to include cultural and arts facilities Subsidise cultural and art activities -> provide job opportunities to young people with artistic talent and creativity Sports industry Promotes sport development in Hong Kong by Promoting community sports Supporting elite sports Developing Hong Kong into a centre for major international sports events -> Promotes development of Hong Kong sports industry -> Attract tourists and increase demand for related support services -> more employment opportunities 3.2 Challenges ¶ Low educational levels -> lower incomes Jobs in knowledge economy requires a high level of education May only be able to take up low-skilled jobs and earn lower incomes Need to grasp multiple skills Constantly learn news skills to meet the needs of job market (Science and technology) Intensifying competition among people with high education levels More university and college degrees -> Keen competition Mismatch of job Highly educated may need to accept jobs that don't match their academic qualifications and majors -> Mismatch between academic qualifications and positions 3.2 Future trends ¶ Emerging industries ¶ Emerging industries AI developing rapidly -> application expands to different fields -> Became increasingly computerised and automated -> Improves the business model and production efficiency Creating new occupations AI technology increasingly mature Can create new products and services and derive new jobs and businesses Would create 130M new jobs and occupations Replacing some types of jobs Low skilled jobs and repetitive jobs will be replaced by AI technology Also assist in analysing complex data and making accurate decisions -> technical tasks ( data analysis : accounting, legal consulting, financial analysis) may be replaced by computers Changes in employment patterns Map not be satisfied with lifestyle of one occupation Gig economy : Freelance workers use websites or applications to sign short form contracts with employers to provide services and earn income e.g. Food deliveries , translators, writers Opportunities More freedom : choose their own working hours, locations, and types -> achieve work-life balance More satisfaction : Work different jobs based on their interests Diverse work experience : Work for different organisations, engage in different types of jobs -> helps develop skills and gain diversified work experience Challenges Unstable income: Do not have a fixed monthly income, may need to work multiple jobs to pay daily expenses Lack of labour protection Do not have a formal employment relationship with companies -> do not provide employee benefits and protections Unfavourable for career development Jobs are low skilled and replaceable May not be favourable for future job hunting Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area ¶ Opportunities Employment opportunities Enterprises have huge demand for highly educated and skilled talents Can choose suitable jobs for their own career development in the region Entrepreneurship opportunities Established Youth Development funds: subsidise Hong Kong non-gov organisations to provide entrepreneurial support services to Hong Kong young people starting their own business Challenges Difficulty of adaptation Adapt to different living and working cultures Need to have good Putonghua skills to communicate and integrate Keen competition Need to have knowledge, skills and creativity to stand out Lack of understanding Systems are different Lack of understanding of mainland laws and business systems Unfamiliar with region's development planning , policies and industry ecology -> difficult to grasp development opportunities

industries grew rapidly and peaked Small in scale, mainly for export Distribution Along both sides of Victoria harbour Expanded to urban fringe and new towns Stages 1950s Chinese immigrants = labour Textile and plastic industry Found along Victoria harbour (Hung Hom) 1960s-mid1970s Light industries (garment, toys, watches, clocks, electronics) Multi-storey factory built on urban fringe (Kwun Tong) mid 1970s - mid 1980s Industries need larger space (food processing, machinery manufacturing, printing) Gov. built industrial zones and industrial estates in new towns (Sha Tin, Yuen Long) late 1990s - present Supports development of high-tech industries (ICT, AI, biotech) Close to universities Coastal locations ( good working env ) 2.2 Change of manufacturing industry of Hong Kong ¶ Relocated from Hong Kong to ZDR(Zhujiang Delta Region) then moved further away to Cities in Guangdong Production Mode Single-point production mode Both headquarters and factories: same place Multi-point production mode / 'front shop, back factory' production mode Headquarters in Hong Kong: Management, product design, marketing, logistics Factories in ZDR : production, assembling, packaging Decline in importance Less important to Hong Kong's economy GDP decreased from 30% (1970) -> 1% (2020) % of people employed also declined Tertiary industry became the most important 2.3 Push and pull factors ¶ Push factor : motivate industries to leave Pull factor : encourage industries to move in Wage Hong Kong: Rising wages -> increased production costs Large population in ZDR -> abundant supply of cheap labour Reduce production costs Rent Hong Kong Land supply limited -> High rents Multi-storey factory building still expensive ZDR Extensive flat land at lower costs -> larger factories at lower costs Government support HK: non-intervention policy -> lacked support and incentives Chinese Government Special Economic Zones in Shenzhen in 1978 during economic reforms Incentives offered to attract Hong Kong manufacturers to invest in ZDR Pollution control Hong Kong Strict Required sewage facilities ZDR Loose Not required -> Lower production costs 3 Global Shift of Manufacturing ¶ 3.1 Industrial belt ¶ Where traditional industrial regions cluster Found in mid-latitudes of the northern hemisphere Spans Europe , East Asia , North America Heavy industries (iron and steel) are major types of manufacturing activities Light industries (textile) are less Europe United Kingdom Industrial revolution Textile and iron and steel industry thrived Spread to other part of Europe (Ruhr Region in Germany) Eastern Europe St. Petersburg, Russia Spread to Moscow, Ukraine Japan, Korea, China : traditional industrial centres in East Asia Eastern coast of Kanto Plain in Japan (Tokyo) Seoul and Busan in Korea Three Northeast Provinces and Beijing-Tianjin Region in China North America Great Lakes Region : iron and steel , car making 3.2 Locational factors for industrial belt ¶ Physical Large area of cheap and flat land Cities along are rich in natural resources -> raw materials and energy resources Human Big cities nearby -> markets , capital and labour Good transport network and facilities e.g. railways and ports Carry out policies that support industrial development Agglomeration economies Similar industries cluster in an area Share infrastructure Save production costs (shipbuilding factories buy steel in bulk for low costs from steel plant nearby ) Supporting services are bought in ( banking , insurance ) Workers with different skills are attracted Industrial inertia Even if locational advantages are lost industries stay because: stable and availability of markets , facilities and labour Reduced risk of relocation 3.3+3.4 Global Shift of Manufacturing ¶ Industrial belt have relocated to new industrial regions New industrial regions Low-skilled production process moved from More developed countries (MDCs) to Less developed countries (LDCs) e.g. Southeast Asia, Central America New industrial regions emerged Change in manufacturing output value LDCs undergone rapid industrial development -> LDCs share in global manufacturing output increased significantly MDCs declined, some MDCs experience industrial decline China has been the fastest growing nation Overtook everyone else and became the 'world factory' Causes ¶ Technological advancement Overcame geographical barriers Save production time -> Increases mobility of goods and people Transport Good transport facilities -> reduce costs e.g. Modern container ships have a large capacity Transport bulk amount at low costs -> heavy industry not bounded by source of raw material and energy Air transport fast means to ship products Allows people to travel between places easily -> manage business Production technologies Give industries more freedom Steel plant can reuse scrap iron -> can be located further from iron mines Refrigeration and preservation tech -> food processing can be located further from market Breakthroughs in ICT (email, video conferences) -> speed up information exchange between headquarters and regional offices Labour cost reduction LDCs have abundant supply of cheap labour -> attract many labour intensive and low tech industries Wages of well-educated professionals are cheaper in LDCs -> high-tech companies set up R&D centres in India Market reduction LDCs undergone rapid economic development -> Demand of consumer goods increase Become new markets for manufactured products Political considerations Favourable policies LDCs set up industrial parks Provide manufacturers with various economic incentives ( Lower tax rates , priority in power supply , relaxed pollution control politics ) Reduction of trade barriers Countries impose tariffs or quotas on imported goods -> protect local industries -> foreign companies set up factories in these countries to reduce trade barriers Nike set up factories and retail stores in LDCs -> trade barriers are overcome -> TNCs (transnational corporations) play important part in global shift of manufacturing 3.5 Role of TNCs in Global Shift of Manufacturing ¶ Transnational corporations (TNCs): have factories and offices in many countries production mode Multi-point production mode by division of labour Headquarters are located in MDCs (home countries) Regional offices and R&D centres : other MDCs Factories : LDCs (host countries) Through FDI ( foreign direct investment ) Responsible for low-skilled prod process such as assembling Case: Nike TNC based on Oregon, USA Moved factories to docs.text: Technological advancement Overcame geographical barriers Save production time -> Increases mobility of goods and people Transport Good transport facilities -> reduce costs e.g. Modern container ships have a large capacity Transport bulk amount at low costs -> heavy industry not bounded by source of raw material and energy Air transport fast means to ship products Allows people to travel between places easily -> manage business Production technologies Give industries more freedom Steel plant can reuse scrap iron -> can be located further from iron mines Refrigeration and preservation tech -> food processing can be located further from market Breakthroughs in ICT (email, video conferences) -> speed up information exchange between headquarters and regional offices Labour cost reduction LDCs have abundant supply of cheap labour -> attract many labour intensive and low tech industries Wages of well-educated professionals are cheaper in LDCs -> high-tech companies set up R&D centres in India Market reduction LDCs undergone rapid economic development -> Demand of consumer goods increase Become new markets for manufactured products Political considerations Favourable policies LDCs set up industrial parks Provide manufacturers with various economic incentives ( Lower tax rates , priority in power supply , relaxed pollution control politics ) Reduction of trade barriers Countries impose tariffs or quotas on imported goods -> protect local industries -> foreign companies set up factories in these countries to reduce trade barriers Nike set up factories and retail stores in LDCs -> trade barriers are overcome -> TNCs (transnational corporations) play important part in global shift of manufacturing
docs.title: Causes

docs.text: Transnational corporations (TNCs): have factories and offices in many countries production mode Multi-point production mode by division of labour Headquarters are located in MDCs (home countries) Regional offices and R&D centres : other MDCs Factories : LDCs (host countries) Through FDI ( foreign direct investment ) Responsible for low-skilled prod process such as assembling Case: Nike TNC based on Oregon, USA Moved factories to Japan, Korea and Taiwan increasing production costs -> further relocated to other LDCs where labour costs are lower e.g. Thailand , China and Vietnam Advantages Allows TNCs to make good use of locational advantages -> reduce prod cost + expand markets Promotes global capital flow and technology transfer -> boosts industrial development of LDCs

docs.text: More ambitious and powerful -> started a new wave of colonial expansion and actively built colonies in Asia and Africa Background Ambition enhanced by early colonial expansion Competed to build overseas trading footholds and colonies -> European-centred world trading system was formed Economic exploitation -> Wealth -> More ambitious to expand overseas Existing footholds became bases Independence of colonies in the Americas US declared ' Monroe Doctrine ': No longer be regarded as targets of colonisation -> Sought to build new colonies in Asia and Africa after losing them Supremacy of European countries Technological and military strength increased Traditional Asian power (e.g. China, India) began to decline Southeast Asian and African countries are weak Difference in national power -> ambition to expand into Asia and Africa Main reasons Economic Strong demand for resources and markets Industrial revolution -> find raw materials , markets and investment opportunities overseas Expanded colonial rule to develop and consolidate economic interests Huge population and resources in Asia and Africa Cheap labour and raw materials (e.g. Cotton in India, Copper and diamonds in Africa) -> fuelled European ambitions to scramble for Asia Political Limited room for expansion in Europe Nationalist revolutions -> Germany and Italy were unified Map of Europe largely took shape -> limited room to expand -> expanded abroad Rise and development of nationalism Nationalism arose in Europe Advocated national independence and gaining national wealth and glory by overpowering others -> Urged to speed up aggression against others Carried out colonial expansion to gain national glory and enhance international influence Social and cultural aspects 'White man's Burden' spread in Europe Believed it was their duty to educate the inferior Asians and Africans ( non-white people ) Some missionaries supported overseas expansion in order to spread Christianity to Asia and Africa

European countries Sovereignty: European countries Replaced existing governments Appointed colonial officials to rule directly e.g. Vietnam (Asia) Economical Resources exploitation Natural resources Plundered natural resources -> used as raw materials / exported Britain: Gold and diamonds in South Africa Spain: Silver and minerals in Mexico Land resources Built plantations Forced to grow cash docs.text: On Europe Forming a European-centred world trading system Set up huge colonial empires Exported industrial products at high prices -> promoted industrial development -> development of for control of colonies in North America) On the Colonies Political Modernisation Carried out reforms in response to European colonial expansion e.g. Japan which became a world power after successful reforms European countries introduced Western modern administrative systems Improved local governance Western parliamentary and Judicial systems -> spirit of the rule of law Some colonies (e.g. Malaysia) kept the colonial administrative and judicial system , after independence from colonial rule Discrimination and oppression Characterized by racial discrimination Faced unfair political treatment European colonists had great political power and appointed as major officials Local people did not share real power and could only become junior officials Some adopted high-handed policies : Suppressed colonized people by force Economic Infrastructure improvement Improved transport system by building roads , railways and piers e.g. India has the fourth largest railway network in the world owing to British Many economic activities were also developed Economic exploitation Plundered natural resources , monopolized plantations , mines , oil wells Slave trade reduced workforce in Africa -> Economic development lag behind Mainly developed agriculture and mining , ignored industry in their colonies -> Hindered the colonies' long term economic development Destruction of traditional economy Built large plantations and forced colonies to grow cash crops ( rubber , pepper ) Sold surplus industrial goods to the colonies -> decline of local handicraft industries Destroyed traditional self-sufficient economy Greatly reduced farmlands for growing food -> famines Social and cultural Improvements in education and living standards Europeans introduced modern education , Western ideas , receptor, temperature receptor, pressure receptor and pain receptor Stimulated -> send signals to the brain through nerves -> interprets and produces senses we experience Sensitivity to touch sensory hair cells surrounded by a gel-like structure and a fluid 3 of them lies on a different plane at right angles to each other -> detect movements of head in different directions Head moves -> fluid moves and stimulates the sensory hair cells Send signals through nerves to the brain -> interprets it to determine the position and movements of the head -> Interprets the signals to produce response Responsible for intelligence , memory and thinking Medulla Controls basic life functions (e.g. Heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure) Cerebellum Coordinates muscles to produce body movements docs.text: Role of our brain Sense organs : responsible for detecting stimuli and sending signals to the brain brain: integrates and interprets the signals -> produce senses Decides on what actions to take -> send signals to the muscles through nerves -> response Reaction time -> time between detecting a stimulus and making a response Takes time for brain to receive signals from the sense organs , interpret the signals then make a response Parts of the brain Cerebrum Integrates and interprets the signals from sense organs Send signals to muscles to make response Responsible for intelligence , memory and thinking Medulla Controls basic life functions (e.g. Heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure) Cerebellum Coordinates muscles to produce body movements Maintains body balance Illusions Brain interprets signals incorrectly -> illusion
docs.title: 10.7 Brain and our senses

docs.text: Coordination ( between sense organs , brain and muscles ) are important Some substances (e.g. alcohol , drugs , organic solvents ) can affect this coordination Abusing can have harmful effects Drinking alcohol e.g. Beer, wine, spirits Affects Slow down our reaction to stimuli (longer reaction time ) Leads to blurred vision and unclear speech Long term drinking can damage brain and liver Affects judgement and memory Causes addiction Causes difficulty with body coordination Taking drugs Chemical substances that can affect our body functions Use drugs in a incorrect way for non-medical purposes -> drug abuse Some people take illegal drugs -> extremely harmful: Damages organs , may lead to deaths e.g. Cocane ( coke ), Cannabis ( weed ), Methylamphetamine ( ice ), heroin , MDMA ( ecatacy ), Ketamine Harms Blurred vision Loss of appetite -> malnutrition Permanent damage to organs Brain Addiction hallucination poor judgement and memory slow reaction sleep problems Skin sores Uncontrolled shaking of head and limbs Frequent and painful urination Unable to control urination Reasons Wrongly believe can get relief from boredom and stress Because of peer pressure Bad inhaling organic solvents e.g. thinner , glue , correction pen by inhaling the vapour Reach the brain -> affect senses and judgement May become excited and violent -> hurt themselves and others Permanently damage many organs , may even lead to death

docs.text: Factors for the First World War ¶ Conflicts among European powers Extreme nationalism Expand aggressively -> Enhance status and influence at any cost Intensified disputes e.g. Germany ('Pan-Germanism') <-> France (Recapture Alsace-Lorraine, Avenge defeat in Franco-Prussian War) Austria-Hungary (Suppress national independence, expand territory) <-> Russia and Serbia ('Pan-Slavism', establish 'Greater Serbia' in Balkan Penisula) Alliance system Triple Alliance (Central powers) Germany , Austria-Hungary , Italy (1882) To isolate France Triple Entente (Allied powers) France , Britain , Russia (1907) -> Divided into two rival camps , Turn into large-scale wars with chain reaction of Allies' intervention Scrambling for colonies -> Conflicts Incident Power Description Tunisian Incident France, Italy French occupied Tunisia , Italy protested Fashoda Incident Britain, France In Sudan , divided their sphere of influence Moroccan Crises ... ... Armaments racer Believed Strong military force could safeguard national security and interests Introduced conscription to expand armies -> Increased military expenditures Developed new weapons of mass destruction (e.g. machine guns) Built " Dreadnoughts " (large warships) mainly Britain and Germany -> Reluctant to make concessions in case of conflicts Pre-war Crises First Moroccan Crisis (1905-1906) Kaiser William II visited Morocco and declared its sovereign independence -> Discontent with France Forced to make a concession: Recognise French privileges in Morocco at last Second Moroccan Crisis (1911) France sent troops to Morocco to put down riots Germany sent gunboats to Agadir -> Morocco became a French protectorate -> Relation between Germany and France worsened Bosnian Crisis (1908) Ottoman Empire was in decline -> Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina (Blocked their expansion) Serbia and Russia wanted to expand -> Finally gave in bc Austria-Hungary was supported by Germany Serbs form a anti-Austrian organisation -> assassination in Sarajevo Two Balkan Wars Ottoman Empire lost a large part of European territory Austria-Hungary wanted to stop Serbia from expanding -> Supported Albania's independence -> Prevented Serbia from gaining access to the sea -> Straining relationship First Balkan War Balkan League ( Serbia , Bulgaria , Montenegro , Greece ) VS Ottoman Empire Balkan states seized the European territories of the Ottoman Empire Second Balkan War Balkan League except Bulgaria , Ottoman Empire , Romania VS Bulgaria Bulgaria was dissatisfied with the distribution of land after the war -> Bulgaria was defeated Outbreak of the First World War ¶ The Sarajevo incident ( 1914 ) Archduke Franz Ferdinand (heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary)
